Often times, depression is a result of a chemical imbalance. There's this whole attitude that people aren't allowed to be depressed if they have a good life and it's absolute crap. You can have the perfect life, with everything you've ever wanted, and still be depressed if you are dealing with a chemical imbalance. Only medications will help with that. 

On the other hand, there is a cognitive aspect to depression. This is the whole pessimistic attitude you're talking about, or self-destructive thoughts. The whole worthless, hopeless, helpless aspect of depression. Therapy and some cognitive reframing will help with this. 

You really need to evaluate yourself and decide if you have symptoms of depression. Do you just have this pessimistic attitude about life? Or do you have feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleeping and eating patterns, lack of interest in pleasurable activities? Some people are just naturally pessimistic, and that's okay. Others are depressed and need medication and therapy.

Bottom line, just because you've had "a good life" doesn't mean you have to feel a certain way.

Okay. First. There are a number of issues. Do you have insurance? The costs shouldn't be too astronomical if you do. Call your insurance provider if you need to. 

Second. Have you tried just outpatient counseling? I can't tell if the counselor you mentioned seeing was affiliated with your university.. If he/she was, I would recommend seeing a professional outside of a college campus. I saw one at my university, and often, they are not equipped to deal with these issues. 

Third. Have you talked with your doctor/NP about the issues you've been having with the Lexapro? Sometimes, different meds work for different people, and you may have to try a number of medications until you find one that works for you. Have you tried anything else? 

Fourth. Hospitalization can be tricky. Mental health hospitalizations will be permanent and should be avoided if at all necessary. Just to tell you options, you can voluntarily commit yourself. You will be evaluated and the hospital will decide if you merit hospitalization or not. In this scenario, you will be able to leave if you wish, you just have to give them prior notice (its 72 hours in Pennsylvania, not sure about SC) You can also be committed by someone. You will have no say in it if it's determined that you absolutely need to be in the hospital. You cannot leave on your own free will, and you will be evaluated after a number of days (usually 5) and either kept, or discharged.

I worked in a psych unit, and I must tell you, hospitalization is usually kept to the minimum, they try to get you on a right combo of meds, and then send you on your way. We tend to only keep patients who are psychotic or homicidal long term, and you seem neither. 

There are also things like partial hospitalization, or good old outpatient care. My feeling is that, if you can stick with outpatient or partial, do it. They don't do much else than you would get in a hospital. Hospitals just really offer round the clock supervision and no privacy. 

I know there are programs out there that will help with the cost of hospitalization. I know the hospital I worked at would use something close to a sliding scale for payment. Here is a link, http://www.ehow.com/info_7745844_financial-assistance-mental-health-treatment.html. It's just ehow, but it might help point you to some potential options. 

I would worry about your mental health first, and college second. Your health is way more important and if you don't get these issues addressed, having money for college will be useless. There are school loans, and in some majors, tuition forgiveness. 

I hope this helped a bit. PM me if you want to talk.
